rationale: A wins because it keeps speculation on a leash: "Mercury says it's profitable on 200,000 businesses. Consumer banking will test that claim" turns missing economics into an honest reporting question. B has real bones, especially "Mercury Is Offering Consumer Accounts Without a Bank Charter," but it keeps stepping over the facts with lines like "It Just Started Pitching Them Personally" and the flatly unsupported "Two Years After SVB." That's not edge; that's a fact-check bill waiting to arrive.
gaps_in_A: "The launch is live today" assumes exact launch-day status from "is launching"; if this is not already public at 2026-06-09T16:00:00Z, the decay math is too aggressive.

"Mercury wants to hold consumers' money without being a bank" is a strong hook but legally sloppy shorthand; the facts say partner banks provide the banking services, so this needs tighter wording before a regulation reporter sees it.

"what Mercury Personal does that existing consumer accounts don't" asks for differentiation the update does not provide; without an answer, the neobank/incumbent angle becomes a routine market-entry item.
gaps_in_B: "Two Years After SVB" is not grounded in the supplied timeline and is wrong against the 2026 current date; opening with bad date math is how a pitch dies in the subject line.
"Mercury's name recognition was built entirely on being the startup-banking alternative" turns "became well known" into a monocausal brand claim. That word "entirely" is doing unpaid invention.

"Mercury's playbook runs opposite to the consumer-to-business neobank trajectory most competitors have tried" invents a market pattern the update never supplied; the angle even admits it needs comparables.

"Mercury Has 200,000 Business Customers. It Just Started Pitching Them Personally" asserts existing-customer targeting and cross-sell that are not in the facts. A waitlist is not the same thing as a business-customer funnel.
